articles.text: Take City Hall out of mix for housing Editor: Thank you for providing the Housing Element FAQ (https:// www.piedmontishome.org/faqs). I found it very helpful. At this time, I have one recommendation: Do not include 120 Vista Avenue (City Hall, Fire Department) in the Housing Element. When school is in session, there are times when traffic and parking are severely affected. If I need to drive to Mulberry’s or the Bank of America ATM at such a time, my progress will be reduced to a crawl, and I probably will not be able to find parking nearby. If 120 Vista is converted to multifamily housing without off-street parking, traffic and parking in the area will be an order of magnitude worse during most hours of every day. The need to replace inadequate city facilities at 120 Vista is a separate issue. New facilities should be planned and financed in a manner similar to that being used to replace the city’s pool. articles.text: 10th Annual Piedmont Artisanal Beer Festival is October 7 The Piedmont Center for the Arts will host one of its most popular events of the year the first weekend of October. On Friday, October 7, the 10th Annual Piedmont Beer Festival will take over the Center for the Arts for a celebration of Artisanal brewers and their finest home brews. In addition to sampling the best of local home brewers, guests are invited to have a legitimate German dinner on the lawn in front of the Center, with freshly grilled bratwurst, potato salad and red cabbage. Food is provided by Dave Larson at Piedmont Grocery. A panel of Piedmont celebrity judges will award prizes to home brewers for Best Pale Ale, Best Lager, Best Porter, Best IPA, and Best in Show. This year’s celebrity judges are Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, and Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson. Brewers already registered include Piedmont brewers Matt Gerhardt, Carter Dunlap, Trevor Fleshman, Zachary Jones, Ed Sweeney and Case Gardner. In addition, a 2021 winner, Kyle Blomseth, has also signed up. He won last year’s best specialty beer with a Belgian Style Ale. To enter home brews, contact Center for the Arts board member Carter Dunlap at carter@dunlapclan.net, or Jay Russell at jayrussell35@gmail.com. Include your name, phone & e-mail address and the type of beer you will bring. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue at the corner of Bonita Avenue.

articles.text: After two years of meeting teachers through Zoom, it was wonderful to return to the classroom for Back-to-School night this year. We felt especially heartened to hear from teachers about how they plan to incorporate social justice and identity into the curriculum, from reading diverse, award-winning books to exploring geography, culture and current events through multiple perspectives. Many parents in the community didn’t have the fortune of a multicultural education when we were growing up. Now our children do. Our children are still learning literary analysis, the components of persuasive essays, critical developments in world and U.S. history — the nuts and bolts at the core of their education. But they’re doing so through a wider, more inclusive and equitable lens. Including diverse perspectives doesn’t mean sacrificing the quality of their education. Rather, it increases rigor, helping our children open up their field of view beyond Piedmont. Improving the educational experience for all students in the community isn’t as easy as flipping a switch. It takes time, training, funds, resources and planning — especially if we want to do this work well. For this reason, the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) advocated for a Director of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion. A new position in Piedmont School District. That position has been filled by Dr. Marguerite Wyngaard, and we are thrilled to include her as an important part of our community. We believe her leadership, expertise and guidance are critical and necessary in navigating the challenge of creating a more culturally diverse learning experience. Students must prepare to be active members of an increasingly multicultural community, to live, work and grow within that community. Piedmont’s efforts to incorporate diversity, equity and inclusion in schools means that we are cementing our commitment to academic excellence. Join PADC for its next general meeting in September. articles.text: On Thursday, September 1, this reporter walked down memory lane at Piedmont High, his alma mater, to do an Inside the Classroom feature on Melanie McCauley’s Yearbook class. Instead of merely observing, McCauley called me to the front of the class to go over the basics of reporting, interviewing, camera operations, privacy law and caption writing. The production of the Yearbook requires its staff to be at every important school function during the year, with emphasis on taking plenty of photos and writing captions for each. I began my talk with a couple of tips on the use of the Post’s Nikon camera. The camera was passed to Sohrab “Seb” Ford to take some photos for the story. Hoping to save the future journalists from future woes, I pointed out how to change out the lens which has reverse threads and abides by “Lefty Tighty, Righty Loosey.” Another helpful tip was learning to use “Aperture Priority Mode” on the camera for preventing blurred photos when there is motion. We moved on to a discussion of California’s laws on consent to record people and “fair use” for taking photos in public. I demonstrated how we do the Question Man feature in the paper by invitPhotos by Seb Ford Reporter Jay Russell demonstrates to Piedmont High School students in Melanie McCauley’s Yearbook class how to attach a long lens to a camera. ing six students to be subjects of Question Man this week, allowing them to see how to politely, but effectively get candid answers in public. After students browsed through the paper, questions arose. “How much does this size of advertisement cost,” asked senior Ginger Gardner. “For a photo caption of a group, how many people do you need to identify by name?” asked McCauley. I explained that the Post does its best to identify everyone pictured by first and last name, but that for groups six or more, often the caption will be general and not include the names of everyone. The glaring exception is the inclusion of names of all the people pictured in the weekly Walking on Wednesdays articles. My visit ended with some irony, as I scooted aside some of the brand-new computers in the STEAM lab classroom to plug in my 1986 Brother Typewriter. Students lined up to try their hands on the archaic device. I challenged them to write one sentence each, and to keep a narrative going based upon the previous sentence. The students had a little too much fun writing about friends and the difficulty of Mr. Savage’s science courses. So much so, that when it came time for McCauley Staff Photo Melanie McCauley talks to her students about the events they will be covering for the high school yearbook this year. The Post’s Question Man, Jay Russell, asks senior Edin Lorin the Question of the Week while Yearbook students take part in a discussion.

articles.text: Storytelling is an important part of early childhood development. School is back in session and everyone is learning their math, science, language arts skills and hopefully some play. My favorite part of school has always been story time. This activity happens in the classroom at all age levels, from circle time for the littles all the way to Socratic seminars for the bigs. Storytelling is important from the very beginning of life. There is much research stating that storytelling is key for the developing brain including creativity, imagination, vocabulary and communication. This early exposure to letters, words and structure help children to read and write. Almost more importantly, storytelling and sharing aids children in telling their own stories allowing them to process and understand their own experiences, often reflecting their culture, language and history, contributing to the formation of identity. At Fairyland I watch children enjoying the stories being told at the puppet theatre. So much is manifesting in a short 15-minute show — the recognition of a story with characters, values, emotions and drama. This is evidenced by laughter, clapping, gasps and questions. As they build language The puppet show at Children’s Fairyland in Oakland. and communication, stories also spark curiosity and engage us in realities other than our own. This trip into another reality gives us valuable perspective on our own experiences. What can you do to support storytelling in your little people? • Talk a lot. For babies and toddlers, narrate what you are doing or what you will be doing and integrate voice inflection to help the story flow. • Share who you are. Tell family histories or stories illustrating who you are as a unit. • Write it down. Take dictation from your young storyteller and read it back to them. It often grows or gets clarified. • Act it out. Help young storytellers dramatize the stories they tell by adding movement. Although the structured environment of language arts in the classroom is crucial, storytelling outside of the classroom is also important. Storytelling directly impacts the development of our children, and the effects have a powerful impact on our community. Kymberly Miller is the Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, the mission of which is to spark imagination, learning, and development through the poer of storytelling. Article reprinted from Piedmont Post in October 2021.

articles.text: PHS tops Mission San Jose, Clayton Valley, Newark Memorial, Cal High Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team started its season with a bang on Friday and Saturday, September 2-3, defeating four teams in the Labor Day Bash to claim the tournament title. Their victories opened with a 15-7 win over Mission San Jose on Friday, then 7-4 over Clayton Valley in the second round. They trampled Newark Memorial 13-5 in the semifinals, and then closed with a sudden-death overtime victory over California High, 10-9. Their finals victory featured rallying from a 9-6 deficit in the fourth period. George Stein scored the tying goal with 11 seconds left, and Declan Linnane scored the game-winner with 2:47 left in overtime. “It comes down to grit and determination. The entire team showed that,” said head coach Rik Krumins. “The fourth game in a tournament is always challenging physically. There were a lot of things not going on our way in the beginning of the game, but they really turned it around and stuck to the game plan as we made adjustments. Cal High played a press and we made adjustments late in the second. Things started turning around in the fourth quarter,” he said. Linnane was named tournament’s Most Valuable Player after scoring nine goals, four assists, and four steals. Peter Krumins and George Stein also earned first-team all-tournament honors. “They were all interchangeable and Declan really started taking over the finals game. Our motion on offense was on point; we were driving in the right position and were making the correct passes. We talked a lot about doing the little things to become successful, and the whole team stepped up to do them,” added Krumins. 10-9 finals win over Cal High Quincy Scherman scored the opening goal after nearly four minutes of action, but Cal High took the lead with a pair of goals in the final minute of the first quarter, including one as the buzzer sounded at the quarter’s end. In the second quarter, Cal High went ahead 3-1 after drawing a man-advantage and was up 4-1 with 3:37 to play. Finn Burke made it 4-2 for PHS but Cal High took a 5-2 lead by halftime. Cal High extended its lead to 6-2 two minutes into the third period, and Stein chipped away at the lead to 6-3 after PHS drew a penalty with 4:54 to go. The Grizzlies answered with a goal a minute later, but Krumins scored for 7-4 with 2:31 remaining. Krumins scored again less than a minute later for a 7-5 score, but Staff Photo Declan Linnane earned the tournament Most Valuable Player award. Photo by Nancy Brahm George Stein earned first-team all-tournament honors. Piedmont’s water polo team got its season started in a big way, winning the Labor Day Bash tournament with four wins, including a sudden-death overtime 10-9 win over Cal High. Cal High scored against 15 seconds later at 1:30. Stein scored after 13 seconds for 8-6, but Cal High put one in with 30 seconds on the clock to retain a 9-6 lead heading into the final period. In the final period, Piedmont’s comeback began when Linnane netted one with 5:06 remaining. With 2:30 left, Stein scored with a man-advantage to make it 9-8. And then with just 11 seconds on the clock, PHS drew another penalty, allowing Stein to tie the match at 9-9. Piedmont won the sprint at the start of the three-minute sudden-death overtime and quickly called a timeout. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team swept Hayward 3-0 on Wednesday, August 31 by scores of 25-6, 25-11, 25-13. It marked their fifth victory after winning four matches the previous week in a tournament in Morro Bay. There’s a clear difference in the attacking mindset in this year’s team. “Our focus right now is utilizing every opportunity from every player. We’ve been working on back row attacks, quick balls outside, right side, and the middle. Nothing is going to be vanilla,” said coach Maria Cardenas. Piedmont’s kills have clear velocity on them, another big change from the previous season. Cardenas’ message to the team through their offseason training has been to hit the ball as hard as possible. “I don’t care if it hits the wall or breaks a window all the way up in the ceiling. I want them ripping the ball; I want them fast and I want them to hit it hard. I want them to continue working on that fast-paced ball,” explained Cardenas. Middle hitter Bree DeYoung reiterated that they’ve been working on putting more pace on their shots, while also keeping successful defensive rotation to allow their offense to have more attempts. “We’ve just working on getting balls faster and quicker to our hitters. We’ve worked on our offense as well as our defense; having both sides play well has really helped us,” said DeYoung. There is also a clear fluid style of play for the Highlanders with successful fakes and attacks at the net. “We want to be up in the air and timing our balls better so we can see the court. We’ve been working on getting every player more trick plays. We middles like to have shots closer to the net, but when we switch to the right side, we’ll cross and the middle will go hit a slide,” added DeYoung. Game Recap The Highlanders opened the match with a resounding 25-6 victory in the first set, after jumping in front 8-1. With the score at 10-6, Piedmont reeled off 15 straight points to win the set, which included two aces by Sadie Town and kills by Town, Tara Kothari, Eden Lorin, and Molly Wagener. In the second set, a 25-11 win, PHS and Hayward traded points until the Highlanders held a 7-5 lead. From there, Piedmont scored 12 of the next 13 points to jump ahead 19-8. They closed out Bree DeYoung goes up for a spike against Hayward. Staff Photos Sadie Town makes a kill against the Farmers. the next six points with two kills by Maddy Mullin, and individual spikes by DeYoung and Klara Zietlow. The third 25-13 win, 25-13, started with Piedmont taking a 12-1 lead. Hayward battled to make it 22-13 with four straight points, but Piedmont closed with a nice block by Elena Stevens, a kill by Shelby Cavenaugh, and a Hayward error for the final point. Piedmont shut out by Del Norte, 42-0 By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s varsity football team suffered a 42-0 shutout loss to the visiting Del Norte Warriors last Friday, September 2 at Witter Field. Del Norte from Crescent City is currently among the topranked Division 4 teams in the North Coast Section after reaching last year’s NCS Finals as a Div. 5 (small enrollment) team. Piedmont will also play as a Div. 5 team in non-conference play this year. “Everything is a learning experience,” said first=year coach Jordan Seiden. “A loss is a loss, but I just hope we learn and grow. articles.text: Piedmont’s JV football team lost 35-2 to visiting Del Norte on September 2. Piedmont’s Junior Varsity football team was knocked down by Del Norte 35-2 at Witter Field in the second game of the season on Friday, September 2. Del Norte, from Crescent City in far northern California, dominated early and often with four touchdowns in the first half Athletic Director Bradley Smet, who has taken over as JV coach, commented that Piedmont needed to show more physicality in tackles and blocks to prevent mistakes. “One of the things that we really need to work on next week is our overall physicality and staying lower. Our guys were staying straight up and down and not able to block and tackle properly. That’s why we saw they missed so many tackles,” he said. Piedmont’s defense showed some spirit by preventing a touchdown in the third quarter by tracking down a Del Norte running back after he had sprinted 60 yards downfield. In the fourth quarter, Piedmont’s offense found some success when quarterback Brandon Dicke threw a 32-yard pass to receiver Vincent Arbit. Photos by Sophie Hess Dash Water Worthen turns a reception upfield. However, PHS was eventually stopped when Del Norte intercepted the ball on the one-yard line. Piedmont’s only points came near the end of game when Albert Bellingrath sacked the Del Norte quarterback in the end zone for a safety. “We didn’t have a whole lot of success in the first half,” said Smet. “It was really good to see our kids coming back when we were already down by 28 points, still fighting, still trying to work hard. Not giving up was definitely good to see.” NEXT UP Piedmont (1-1) goes on the road this weekend to Tahoe City to take on North Tahoe High School on Saturday, September 10 in Tahoe City at 10:00 a.m. The Scots’ offense struggled with consistency against an aggressive Del Norte defense.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ golf team begins its season this week, playing a tri-match with Castro Valley and San Leandro at Redwood Canyon Golf Course in Castro Valley on Thursday, September 8. “Our women’s varsity golf team is back in action. The team began practicing in mid-August. We’re focused on building a program that empowers our players to take personal responsibility for their growth both on and off the course,” said Piedmont coach Howard Oliver. Piedmont returns after going 8-4 overall last season, finishing third in the Western Alameda County Conference tournament at the Metro Links Golf Course. Returning to the team are seniors Aryana Fisher, Rahimeen Shah, Krysta Tsukahara, and Eva Wagg. Also returning are sophomores Mei Assalian and Mackenzie Seto-Ngyuen. New players who will be battling for a place in the starting six on the roster are juniors Henley Lorin, Stella Izakson, and Lily Caldwell. The WACC is still dominated by Alameda which has won 17 consecutive league championships – much like the dominance of Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team. Bishop O’Dowd placed second to Alameda in last year’s tournament. “Looking around the league, Alameda and Bishop O’Dowd are still among the top teams, and this season we’re looking to close the gap,” said Oliver. Of Piedmont’s starters, Fisher was the team’s low-medalist in the WACC tournament after shooting an 87 on the 18-hole course. Assailian proved herself as a freshman last season by firing a 92 in the WACC Finals and will be looking to improve. Shah, meanwhile, shot a 99 in the league tournament and Tsukahara rounded out Piedmont’s scoring with a 101. Oliver named Assalian a team captain and pointed out that the standout sophomore recently scored a hole-in-one in a practice round in Alameda. “Mei Assalian achieved the rare feat [of a hole-in-one] in practice on the 8th hole at Corica Park. She joins the boys’ team’s senior captain Max Schleuning as a player to join the “hole-in-one club”,” said Oliver. articles.text: San Francisco Opera presents the world premiere of Berkeley composer Johns Adams’ latest opera, Antony and Cleopatra, on September 10. articles.text: The American Conservatory Theatre (ACT) presents Passengers onstage at the Geary Theatre in San Francisco beginning September 15. The production will run through October 9. Shana Carroll, the creator, director and choreographer of Passengers, is originally from the Bay Area. The production combines contemporary dance with circus acrobatics, weaving together a story that explores a community of strangers. “When first creating Passengers four years ago, it was in great hope and anticipation of one day, finally, bringing it back home to my native Bay Area. The pandemic put that dream temporarily on hold, but I’m thrilled that – a few long-awaited years later – my little train has finally made its way back to its home station in my beloved San Francisco,” said Carroll. “The themes at the heart of this show – of travel, of nostalgia for foreign lands and past eras, of celebrating a ‘ride’ that is unexpected and so often cut too short ­ – have brought new layers of meaning and importance in our post-pandemic era. In many ways it feels we are premiering a whole new show.” The Geary Theater is located at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. Tickets are available by calling the box office at (415) 749-2228, or by purchasing online at https://www.act-sf. org/whats-on/202223-season/ passengers/.
articles.title: ACT premieres Passengers on September 15

articles.text: The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco, now celebrating its 10th anniversary, returns to Piedmont for a concert on Saturday, September 17 at 7:30 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts. Founding members Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon and Clio Tilton will perform a program to include Beethoven’s String Quartet in A minor, op. 132, Mozart’s “Dissonance” String Quartet in C Major, K465, and Caroline Shaw’s “Valencia”. For tickets click on: https://bit. ly/3TpKMUZ. Beethoven’s opus 132 string quartet is from his collection of “late” quartets, written in the final years of his life. In these works, Beethoven turned inward, leaving us with some of his most exquisite and transcendental music. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco opens its 10th anniversary season with a return to Op. 132, the masterpiece that brought these fine musicians together a decade ago. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco is dedicated to bringing chamber music masterworks to diverse audiences. CMS of SF is passionate about concertizing in intimate settings, creating close connections between performers and listeners and cultivating a relationship between music and audiences that extends far beyond the perimeter of the concert hall. Drawing listeners into the lives of the composers and the world of the music, CMS of SF concerts are a favorite destination for both chamber music lovers and those new to the genre. Members of CMS of SF can be heard performing with the San Francisco Symphony, SF Opera, SF Ballet, the San Francisco and New Century Chamber Orchestras, American Bach Soloists, the Oakland Symphony and many others. Founding members Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton came together through their mutual love of the late Beethoven String Quartets. Collaborations have included artists such as Kay Stern, Stephen Prutsman, Jean-Michel Fonteneau and Jodi Levitz. For more information see: www.chambermusicsocietysf.org.
articles.title: Chamber Music Society of SF to perform concert in Piedmont Sept. 17

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre is showing Goddess from the critically-acclaimed team that created New York’s Shakespeare in the Park’s production of Merry Wise. Performances continue through September 25. Goddess is inspired by the myth of Marimba, the goddess of music, and an ancient folktale passed down by many generations across the continent of Africa. According to the folktale, Marimba created the first instruments and was the first to use her voice in song. She is also described as the most beautiful woman who ever existed and an advocate for peace, she refashioned weapons into instruments and opposed the violence of war. The play was conceived by Saheem Ali, based on the book by Jocelyn Bioh. Music and lyrics are by Michael Thurber, and choreographed by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The cast includes Awa Sal Secka, Aaron Patterson, Isio-Maya Nuwere, Grasan Kingsberry, Rodrick Covington, Melessie Clark, Wade Watson and Zachary Downer. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/goddess/. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223 ®

articles.text: Natalie Portman stars in Black Swan. Black Swan is an intense, gripping psychodrama that moves along a precipice between the transcendent art of ballet and a dark decent into madness. The performances are astonishingly good. First, ballet, no matter its patina of delicacy and seemingly fragile beauty, composed of movement to music that stirs and inspires, is also a sport practiced by athletes who give new meaning to the concepts of preparation, brutally hard work, and unflinching commitment. It is this aching sacrifice that is, ultimately, at the center of Black Swan. A young woman, Nina Sayers (Natalie Portman), has been insulated most of her life by the constraints of ballet and by a controlling, domineering mother, Erica (Barbara Hershey). To her astonishment, she is cast as the prima ballerina in the dual role of the black swan (Odile) and the white swan (Odette) in Swan Lake. The role is an obvious metaphor for this young woman, who is naïve, protected, talented, and now challenged by the Director, Thomas Leroy (Vincent Cassel), to explore her dark side, to find the visceral and the real in the role of Odile. When she dances as the white swan she is controlled perfection. But it’s when she dances as the black swan that she is bound by restraint and even fear. Great art, Leroy tells her, means letting go. And so Nina’s metamorphosis begins and the film moves incrementally into layers of brilliant, wrenching dysfunction. What is real and what is delusional becomes increasingly blurred as she descends into a world of such pressure that her ability to cope begins to fray. Hers is a brittle soul in a world that can be harsh; red flags of overwhelming anxiety and madness ignored in the name of an enchanted story about a woman transformed into a swan by a mad sorcerer, a tale elevated to the sublime by the music of Tchaikovsky. But this film is more than a deliberative, psychological study of a compelling, fragmenting character. Black Swan is, at times, unhinged, yet also lovely and compelling. Black Swan. Directed by Darren Aronofsky. Starring Natalie Portman, Mila Kunis, Barbara Hershey, Winona Ryder and Vincent Cassel. 1 hr., 48 min, Rated R. Released in 2010. articles.text: In 1979, James Baldwin, noted author, playwright and essayist, sent a detailed proposal to his agent – some 30 pages long – for a book he titled Remember This House. It was a work of nonfiction that was intended to connect three men: Malcom X, Martin Luther King, and Medgar Evers. Less than 10 years later (1987), Baldwin died, never having written more that those 30 pages. It proved to be, in its own right, a powerful essay on race. Director Raoul Peck used those pages (and some notes and essays) to craft not a biographical documentary about Baldwin, but instead a film about race using Baldwin’s transcendent words. The content was drawn from interviews on television and in print and from countless college podiums and used to frame in I am Not Your Negro an issue that has resisted resolution since the first slaves were brought to Jamestown in 1619. Our national identity is embedded in our response to what has been referred to by some scholars as a “Peculiar Institution,” which, as Baldwin explains, is part of our nation’s desire to create a fantasy that is only applicable to one segment of society, and not to all. The denial of what was perpetrated for three centuries continues to haunt us, a truth that Baldwin returns to time after time in this powerful film. He refers to our unwillingness to grapple with the impact of slavery as our “moral monster,” beginning not only with the antebellum South, but during the decades following the Civil War when segregation and Jim Crow were codified. The war was over, the North won, but the attitudes toward black people were deeply and intractably entrenched. Peck includes as part of the film, stark black and white photos of “Negroes,” a word that Baldwin uses repeatedly, who were lynched with impunity, to include children and men as well as women. What is chilling to the core are the looks on the faces of the men and women who were present at those hangings and bore witness. Their faces flash with a rictus smile, the rising tide of violence and death seemingly irresistible, something that refuses to touch their souls. Peck also reveals that same look, that same rage in the faces of men and women, in footage captured when schools in the South were desegregated. We see a single girl, surrounded by state marshals, making a harrowing journey from the street to the doors of the school building, her bravery beyond description. She is reviled and denigrated and threatened and yet she puts one tentative foot in front of the other. The faces of the protesting crowds are twisted with a hatred that could only be born out of the same impulses that killed Dr. King and Evers, a murderous resistance to our constitutional commitment to civil rights, tempered by the aspirational belief that every person should be judged by the content of their character and not by the color of their skin. It is a concept so elegant and so profound that its beauty is often missed by large segments of society. The national truth is that we have yet to make that journey toward equality, at least not fully. Peck includes contemporary footage of Ferguson, Mo., demonstrating that America’s social fabric continues to be frayed, rooted in slavery. Slavery and all that followed, like a stone dropped into a wide pond, continues to be felt as the ripples move ever outward in concentric circles. The harm done continues. As an aside, James Baldwin, for reasons never fully explored in I am Not Your Negro, chose to leave America and reside in France. But as the Civil Rights Movement began to take form, as men such as Martin Luther King took on its purpose and weight, Baldwin felt its gravitational pull and returned, if only to bear witness to all that was occurring in America as this momentous struggle coalesced. And continues to this day. I am Not Your Negro. Documentary. Directed by Raoul Peck. Narrated by Samuel L. Jackson. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/Netflix/Prime.

You’ve heard his roar, looked into his pink cavernous mouth and took note of those massive canines. And not to forget his incredible strength. Regarding Kong (1933, et al.), all that has changed (other than the narrative, which has been tweaked) is filmmaking technology that has evolved to the point that Kong indeed now looks like the real deal. This incarnation has a different hook, which is actually interesting. It takes place as the Vietnam War is coming to a close. A scientist convinces a senator to send an expedition into the farthest reaches of the South Pacific in search of an uncharted island. Hence, a quasi-military scientific group is formed, consisting of almost a dozen helicopters and a mixed group of soldiers and civilians, to include a war photographer, Mason Weaver (Brie Larson) and a mercenary, James Conrad (Tom Huddleston). This set up lasts some 40 minutes as the choppers skim the tree-tops of this never before seen island. Or so they assume. Suddenly (that’s the operative word for this film), out of the haze they are confronted with Kong and it’s no contest. The choppers are helpless and everyone is in serious harm’s way. Let the games begin. And whatever exposition is delivered at the start of the movie, well that was it. What follows is one very intense escape from Kong Island. It’s all one long, adrenalin-inducing chase across an island where creatures, to include spiders and water buffalo, lizards and birds, are the size of motels. Nothing is as it should be, starting, of course, with Kong. To his credit, what director Vogt-Roberts decides to do make sure that Kong: Skull Island is fun – a real ride. It becomes a long riff on very scary creatures that are intent on snacking on any member of the group that happens to drift away from the others. Of course, there are some subplots that never break the focus of the film. For example, chemistry between Weaver and Conrad is suggested. But there isn’t much time for even a hug. I think they hold hands in a moment of panic, but that’s it. This is about survival, and each scene is, well, breathtaking in a kind of basic way – can they get out of this without too much damage being done? But there is also a Conradian Heart of Darkness aspect to the story (Huddleston/Conrad); even shades of Apocalypse Now are present. (I kept waiting for someone to say they loved the smell of napalm early in the morning.) When the credits rolled at the end, I was glad I saw it. I love movies and I knew this was a big screen film and would not translate to the smaller screen. Kong is after all Kong, and he’s way larger than life. Kong: Skull Island. Directed by Jordan Vogt-Roberts. Starring Brie Larson, Tom Huddleston and Samuel L. Jackson. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on Prime/ HBO Max/Apple tv.

articles.text: A scene from Dreamworks animation’s Turbo. Turbo is a Dreamworks animated feature film, ideal for 7-year-olds. It tells the story of a suburban tomato garden snail named Theo (or Turbo) who considers his life grindingly dull. He is, however, obsessed with the idea of speed. In fact he yearns to be the world’s greatest racer. No surprise, the snails who also live in the garden, a place called the Plant, ridicule Theo when he talks of going faster, especially when he tells them that his hero is Guy Gagné (Bill Harder), an arrogant French world class racer. Despite the doubts of his fellow mollusks, Theo is convinced he will one day compete in the Indianapolis 500, hear the roar of a crowd cheering him on (he’s watched the race on a dusty TV tucked away in a garage), and he’ll do this competing against real human drivers. But not now. Today he is feeling blue after being repeatedly discouraged by his good friend Chet (Paul Giamatti), and almost being run over by a lawn mower. Theo slowly makes his way to a nearby freeway, hoping to watch the cars speeding by. He feels the need for speed. What he’s not prepared for is to be sucked into the engine of a Camaro, a muscle car. Due to this freakish accident, he is saturated in nitrous oxide, which transforms him, to his immense surprise, into a snail with amazing speed akin to the fast and furious. Chet is filled with disbelief until he is snatched by a passing crow but is rescued by Theo who uses his newfound unexpected speed. As a result, the two bros end up in a shopping mall in Van Nuys where they meet a cohort of streetwise snails, voiced by Samuel L. Jackson, Maya Rudolph, Snoop Dogg, Ben Schwartz, and Mike Bell. The gang practices engaging in slowmo races around a very small track in the Starlight Plaza. Theo also gets the help of Tito Lopez and his brother Angelo (Luis Guzman), both humans, who have a food truck at the mall. They get the idea that they might get some publicity for Dos Bros Tacos if Theo can only win the 500. And so, escargot meets street racers – and they’re off to the competition. Keep in mind that the snails can talk to one another but can’t speak to humans. It will take the extraordinary imaginations of the young audience to appreciate a snail in a car race. But the kids will be entertained by Theo, aka Turbo. Turbo. Directed by David Soren. Dreamworks animation. With voices of Ryan Reynolds, Paul Giamatti, Michael Pena. Rated PG. Released in 2013. Now streaming on Prime/peacock/ apple tv.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, September 7, 2022 Features Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers continue to explore million dollar homes By Dick Carter On August 24 members of the Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed looking at some beautiful homes for sale in Piedmont. There were eight homes with listing prices ranging from $2,450,000 to $18,500,000 that the group wanted to see, but they ran out of time and could only walk to five of them. One week later, August 31, the group took a look at the remaining three houses. The first was 317 Sea View Avenue. On the way they observed a Caterpillar land mover carving a hole in the steep hillside in front of a house on Crocker Avenue at the intersection of Wildwood. The house was designed by Albert Farr and built in 1906. At that time a garage was not considered a necessity, and one was not built for the house. Now, 116 years later, that is changing. As the walkers stopped to look, the contractor explained that it is common today for owners of old homes to make a cut in their front yards in order to add a garage. Proceeding past Crocker Park, the group turned onto Sea View and admired the always beautiful flowers in the yard of the Reich family. The yellow dahlias were particularly wonderful. Wednesday Walkers pause for a photo in front of 199 Lafayette Avenue. Pictured are: Larry Olsen Nancy Olsen, Jim Kellogg, Sarah Johnson, Pat Keller, Matt Gerhardt, Ann Quinby, Ian Morgan, Elizabeth Richter, Lisa Euphrat, Phil Witte, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Tally, Charlene Louie, Lois Price, Mary Hedley, Meghan Bennett, Albert Chen, Nadine Guffanti, Alan Goldhammer, Mike Henn, Jim Kuo, Rob Smith, Martin Levy, Brenda Ferrero, Bob Wong, Christen Calliste, Edith Lee, Cheryl Stanton, Peter Persoff, Alicia Rivera, Emma Sangil with K-9 best friend Olive, Dick Carter, and first-time walker Garrett Clifford. We Are Always Accepting New Patients! The group crossed La Salle Avenue and came to 317 Sea View, a 3- bedroom, 3-bath 1,952 square foot home designed by Sidney B. Newsom and built in 1914. This is the first time in 45 years the home is on the market and is listed at $2,450,000. The walkers continued up Sea View and crossed the Oakland-Piedmont city line, where the street becomes Ashmount Avenue. The story was shared of how the city of Piedmont was incorporated with the state in 1907, and its border was geographically defined based on a sewer map. This map was all that was available for the city’s founding fathers, and they used it to beat the city of Oakland’s attempt to annex Piedmont. This sewer map is why Piedmont’s boundary is often irregular with split parcel homes. The group turned on Mandana Boulevard and were quickly back in Piedmont on Crocker Avenue. Another quick left turn put the walkers on La Salle Avenue looking for their next house, 35 Muir Avenue. The Tudor style house was built in 1932 with 5,899 square feet, 5 bedrooms, and 5 bathrooms, with a classic half-timbered façade, a slate roof and an ornamental chimney. The next stop was just up the street at 256 La Salle, a 4-bedroom, 3-bathroom house built in 1922 with 3,765 square feet and in a Spanish Mediterranean design. The home has great views of San Francisco and is listed for $3,595,000. The last stop on the tour was further up La Salle as it becomes Lafayette Avenue. 199 Lafayette is a 3-bedroom/5-bath, 4,583 square foot home, built on .4 acres in 1915. It has views of the Golden Gate Bridge, a pool with a Jacuzzi, and a guest house, and is listed for $5,950,000, The group had completed their walking tour of all the homes on their list, and it was time to get back to their starting point in the city center. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. In my last column I shared some of the winning wines from the Family Winemakers of California tasting held in Oakland. This week finishes coverage of this outstanding event with another batch of winners. On August 21 the Family Winemakers of California held their first ever tasting in Oakland. It is one of my favorite wine events of the year. Many of the people pouring the wine have the same name on their nametags as the name on the wine label. There is a warmth, and yes, love for the wines that you do not find at the more “corporate” wine events. The span of different grape varietals was intriguing. Like to taste a Semillon or a Barbera? How about Tempranillo or Alicante Bouchet? Come on in, they’re all here. I was never really able to find out exactly what constitutes a “family winemaker.” The vast majority of the wineries seemed to span the spectrum from small mom and pop operations to small/ medium size operations making under 10,000 cases per year. As I meandered through the table-filled venue, I focused on small wineries with which I was unfamiliar. There were so many great wines at the tasting – literally hundreds. But the following list catalogues the wines that stood out among a huge sea of also-rans. They are wines of great character and quality and are worth searching out. They show that some of the finest wines in California are created in small, out of the way places by wineries that are fueled by family love and devotion. • 2020 Ca’ Momi Cabernet Sauvignon This Napa Valley Cabernet opens with notes of black cherries, currants plus hints of herbs and dusty soil. Medium to full-bodied, the palate delivers an appealing black fruit mélange with approachable, chewy tannins and a pepper and herbs-laced finish. • 2020 Field Chardonnay Russian River Valley Field has produced a delicious style of Chardonnay with hints of peach, pineapple and citrus blossom. This medium to full-bodied Chardonnay has terrific acidity, to go with the apple and pear fruit and a long finish. A well-balanced wine that is a role model of what California Chardonnay should be. • 2019 Noria Pinot Noir Valentine Vineyard The fruit for this lovely wine comes from the Russian River AVA. Pale to medium purple colored, it smells of black and red cherries, nutmeg and cinnamon followed by nuances of violets, chocolate and earth. Medium bodied on the palate, it is wonderfully elegant and well-poised with effortlessly fragrant red fruit and a long, intense finish. • Berghold Petite Sirah This Petite Sirah hails from the Sierra Nevada foothills. It is dark and brooding with aromas of plums and blackberries. In the mouth it is full-bodied and luscious with boat- • 2018 Lava Cap Petite Sirah Lava Cap is a 40-year-old winery located in the Sierra Foothills blessed with volcanic soils. Their Petite Sirah reveals classic aromas of blueberries, blackberries, smoky oak and earth. Very full-bodied it is packed with dark fruit flavors and a tannic finish. This wine should improve in the cellar for up to two decades. • 2018 Prager “Royal Escort” Port Prager has long been one of the only California wineries specializing in port. The grapes come from a Petite Sirah vineyard in St. Helena. It is made in what in Portugal is called “vintage style” – the biggest, most robust of the ports. It has a beautiful, extravagant bouquet with copious black fruit, spice and hints of menthol and orange rind that unfold wonderfully in the glass. The palate is beautifully balanced with velvety smooth tannins, copious black fruit with a harmonious finish that is a decadent delight. • 2018 Peche Merle Pinot Noir Laguna de Santa Rosa This Russian River Pinot has a classic nose of cherries and cranberries with notes of cola, tea leaves and flowers. Light to medium-bodied, it fills the mouth with warm luscious strawberry jam notes with an integrated vein of baking spice framed by very finely grained tannins and juicy, mouth-watering acidity, finishing long and spicy.

This is my version of a German-style peach kuchen, written on a 3 x 5 inch recipe card in a penmanship style I abandoned decades ago. All to say, I no longer recall the origin of it to give proper acknowledgement. Whilst we are into September, it’s still officially “summer” for a couple more weeks. The farmers at the market say they will likely be harvesting late-crop peach varieties until early October, so there’s time to give this a try. Later you can easily swap out the peaches for another fruit – figs, plums, even apples and pears if this recipe moves you into autumnal fruits. This version yields a soft, tender cake with a soft topping bursting with fruit flavor. articles.text: A History Fair will be held from 11:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. this Saturday, September 10, at the historic Camron-Stanford House at 1418 Lakeside Drive in Oakland. More than 20 Bay Area history-centered organizations and museums will participate. Each organization will have a booth for people to learn more about how to connect to the past. Browse sample exhibits, engage in fun activities, and get a sneak peek at upcoming events. Participating organizations include Peralta Hacienda, USS Hornet Museum, West Oakland Mural Project/Women of the Black Panther Party, and the Friends of Oakland Public Library. Many know the Camron-Stanford House by sight for its proximity to Lake Merritt and to the Main Library across the street. It was built in 1876 and is the last of the beautiful Victorian mansions that once surrounded the lake. Peaches and Cream Cake Makes one 9-inch square cake INGREDIENTS For the cake: • 1-1/2 cup all-purpose flour • 1/4 cup granulated sugar • 1 Tablespoon baking powder • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt • 1 extra-large egg, slightly beaten • 1/2 cup whole milk • 1/3 cup unsalted butter, melted Thoroughly butter a 9-inch square baking pan, or line with parchment paper if you plan to lift the entire cake out of the pan for serving presentation. Use two sheets of parchment paper, placed crosswise in the pan with plenty hanging over the top to easily lift out the cake. Place an oven rack in the center position and preheat the oven to 350° F. In a medium mixing bowl, whisk together the flour, 1/4 cup granulated sugar, baking powder and salt. In a small bowl, combine the first beaten egg, milk, and melted butter. Add the wet mixture to the flour mixture and mix until just combined with no streaks of flour showing. But don’t over mix. Spread this batter evenly into the prepared 9-inch pan and bake for 15 minutes. Meanwhile, prepare the topping by adding the remaining beaten egg, 1/4 – 1/3 cup of granulated sugar, and sour cream together in a small bowl. Mix well. Slice the peaches and set aside. After the initial 15 minutes, remove the partially baked cake from the oven and set on a heatproof surface. Spread the sour cream mixture evenly over the cake then arrange the peaches in a single layer. Sprinkle with cinnamon. Return to the 350° F oven and continue baking for another 15 minutes. articles.text: Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s summer camp in the Sierra foothills since 1931, will have a Campathon fundraiser at Hampton Park this Sunday afternoon, September 11, from 3:00-5:00 p.m. Enjoy Lazy Dog ice cream while completing playstation-style activities that recreate your camp favorites - including a Gaga Ball tournament. Have tons of fun while raising money for many projects at camp. Including a new high ropes pole course. Ask parents, friends, neighbors and extended family members to sponsor you for Campathon. Minimum $100 donation is required per participant. No need to be a camper to participate. During the Campathon complete as many play stations and activities as you want, purchase some ice cream and enjoy reliving camp highlights. The event is also a great way to check out what Augusta is all about and to meet some of its staff members. As a non-profit, the camp needs to raise significant funds to finance a new Ropes Pole Course and support ongoing creative activities at Camp Augusta. One of the most unique aspects of Camp Augusta is the high ropes course elements nestled amongst the pine trees. The trees have been greatly affected by the drought of the last few years and some of the most beloved climbing elements have had to come down for safety. Camp Augusta has a new opportunity to expand and continue to challenge our campers and build confidence and teamwork with the installation of a new Ropes Pole Course. The course will be developed on 85-foot poles to avoid damaging the trees. To donate, sign up at https:// c a m p a u g u s t a . o r g /c a m p a - thon-2022/. articles.text: • Ninja Training Augusta is an ancient training ground for some of the best Ninjas in history… Haven’t heard of them? Exactly… Come and practice the sneaky side of Augusta. • Gaga Ball A classic lunch time game at Augusta. Groups of 9-10 people climb into the “pit” and try to get one another ‘out’ by hitting one another on the legs with a dodgeball. You can’t throw it, you can’t kick it… Come find out how to do it. • Face painting Camp staff members can turn you into a Woodland elf, a fairy, a racoon – anything you want. • Sword Fighting Duels Do you have what it takes to defeat a modern day knight? How about a Camp Director with 20+ years of German Sword fighting experience and a few other staff members in training? Come try a one-onone duel at the park. • Felting Within minutes you can make your very own felted companion. Make a little felt rendition of your favorite pet, human, fungus, plant, flower or extra terrestrial. • Juggling Juggling is something everyone wants to do, though few can. Augusta’s juggling maestros will have you rivaling Cirque du Soleil before you know it. • Wire Jewelry Create your own jewelry with beads and gems and a traditional wire wrapping technique. • Spin Jam Poi, Dart, Diabolo. Fire spinning starts with practice and Spin Jam is the place to be. • Ukulele These little instruments have a lot to show for themselves. They are relatively easy to learn, fun to play and folks can crack out a tune in short order. Ukuleles also happen to travel well and raise spirits wherever they are. • Balloon Twisting Tie your own balloon hat, flower, dog, sword or even a cathedral with an expert balloon tying connoisseur. • Augustan Knowledge Bowl How much do you know about Camp Aug usta?! Test your skills against the most knowledgeable staff at Augusta. • Puppet Making What has three googly eyes, a spiky yellow mohawk, two teeth and a giant purple tongue? Your new puppet. Come make a new sock puppet. • Get Injured Ever wonder what it’s like to have your leg in a cast? Come try it - without the unpleasant part. We’ll bandage you up without having to break something first. A camper created a whimsical sock puppet at last year’s Campathon. and the 10th will tell you “in the universe”! Lazy Dog ice Cream, based in Grass Valley, has been a tradition at Augusta since 2004. Each Monday and Wednesday, the infamous pink truck comes to camp bringing the Augusta exclusive “Drumstick” to the campers (and staff). And now for one day only we are bringing Lazy Dog to Piedmont. Augusta campers in the area will have their chance to get their hands on the best homemade ice cream in the world.

The trails at Middle Harbor Shoreline Park have a great view from every angle. cal facts about the stone training walls along the shoreline. The stone wall (see photo) is a replica of a former historic jetty that was designed in 1874 extending from the Port of Oakland into the bay. The jetties were designed to keep Oakland’s shipping channels open. Prior to their creation, ships had to wait until high tide to enter the shallow waters of the Oakland Estuary. City Hall Chili Cook-off Continued from page 9 was bolstered by many parents and teachers already on campus that evening ahead of Back-toSchool Parents Night. The time of the event, from 5:00-6:00 p.m., also coincided with a girls’ volleyball game on campus which attracted many of their fans to the event. “There was a really good mix of all different community members – adults, kids, teachers and administrators,” said Ruby Guzdar of the 1st place team. Among the competitors was Littlefield’s successor, first-year PHS Principal Sukanya Goswami, who entered a chili under a team name “The Office.” Each guest received three tickets, allowing them to split their votes or give all three tickets (votes) to the same entry. In the event of a tie, the winner would be determined by Rochambeau; a contingency which fortunately, was not needed this year. PHS parent Geoffrey Brennan, who named his concoction Deez Beanz, crafted a crowd-pleasing 2nd place chili, replete with jalapenos and a gourmet cheese topping. The PHS Student Center may have never smelled more welcoming than on August 31 when the Great Chili Cook-off was held. Where in the World Are We? In Paris this summer to celebrate the 50th wedding anniversary of Jaime Austin’s parents, the Deming family took a moment for a keepsake photo in front of the Eiffel Tower. 3 days later both parents had COVID. Pictured perusing the Post far from home are David Deming (left), Ginevra and Ganden Deming, and mom Jaime Austin.
